back: Trade lets a country pay a lower price for imports and receive a higher price for exports than producing everything domestically would allow.
The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country — not necessarily lower absolute cost.
The ability to produce more of a good with the same resources than another country.
Traces comparative advantage to differences in technology between countries.
Traces comparative advantage to differences in relative factor endowments (labor, capital, land) between countries.

front: Economies of scale as a trade benefit?
back: Average production cost falls as output rises with a larger, post-trade addressable market — independent of any comparative-advantage cost difference.
Two-way trade in goods within the same product category or classification, explained by product differentiation under monopolistic competition.
Resources must be reallocated out of import-competing industries; less-efficient firms may exit, displacing workers who may need retraining.
Winners from trade could, in theory, compensate losers and both groups still end up better off in aggregate — not that every stakeholder benefits.
A capital restriction limits openness of financial markets (foreign ownership of domestic assets or vice versa); a trade restriction limits openness of goods markets.
A tax a government levies on imported goods, primarily to protect domestic industries producing the same or similar goods.
A government-imposed limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported, typically for a specified period, administered through import licenses.
A quota-like restriction, but imposed by the exporting country rather than the importer.
A government payment to a firm for each unit of a good it exports, intended to stimulate exports.
A country that is a price taker in the world market for a given good — not necessarily small by population or GDP.

front: Welfare regions A, B, C, D under a tariff or quota?
back: A = producer surplus gain; B+D = deadweight loss (production-side + consumption-side inefficiency); C = government revenue (tariff) or quota rent (quota); A+B+C+D = consumer surplus loss.
CS loss = ΔP × Qd_r + ½ × ΔP × (Qd_ft − Qd_r).
PS gain = ΔP × Qs_ft + ½ × ΔP × (Qs_r − Qs_ft).
Revenue or rent = ΔP × (Qd_r − Qs_r), the price wedge applied to the units still imported after the restriction.
DWL = ½ × ΔP × (Qs_r − Qs_ft) + ½ × ΔP × (Qd_ft − Qd_r) — the irreducible national welfare loss.
Ambiguous: the domestic government (if licenses are auctioned), domestic importers, or the foreign exporter — unlike a tariff, where the government always captures the revenue.

front: Why is a VER often the costliest restriction for the importing country?
back: Because the exporting country administers it, the rent is captured by the foreign exporter by construction, guaranteeing at least the worst-case quota outcome (B+C+D).

front: Small-country export subsidy: effect on domestic price?
back: Domestic price rises to match the higher effective return (world price plus subsidy) producers can earn by exporting.

front: When can a large country gain from imposing a tariff?
back: Only if the exporter cuts its price to retain market share (no retaliation) and the terms-of-trade gain exceeds the large country's own deadweight loss; global welfare still falls.
A group of countries that has agreed to reduce and progressively eliminate barriers to trade — and, in deeper forms, factor mobility — among its members.
Barriers to goods/services trade eliminated among members; each member keeps its own independent policy toward non-members.
An FTA plus a common external trade policy (common external tariff) toward non-members.
A customs union plus free movement of factors of production (labor, capital) among members.
A common market plus common economic institutions and coordinated economic policy among members.
An economic union plus a shared common currency.
Regional integration replaces higher-cost domestic production with lower-cost imports from a fellow member — an efficiency gain.
Regional integration replaces lower-cost imports from a non-member with higher-cost imports from a member (due to the bloc's tariff asymmetry) — an efficiency loss.

front: Two bloc-specific benefits beyond general free-trade benefits?
back: Reduced potential for conflict through greater interdependence, and greater collective bargaining power/political influence than members would have individually.
(1) Cultural and historical differences complicating the political process; (2) constrained scope for independent economic and social policy, most binding in a monetary union.

front: Investment implications of joining a bloc?
back: Upside: lower cost of doing business and greater economies of scale across the bloc. Limitation: persistent taste/culture/competitive differences and contagion risk between members remain.
A rule requiring that a minimum share of the value added in a good sold domestically originate domestically.
A complete prohibition on trade with a specific country.

front: Supplementary: Identity check for tariff welfare calculations?
back: CS loss = PS gain + revenue/rent + deadweight loss — a fast way to catch an arithmetic error.

front: Supplementary: Quota vs. tariff — best-case comparison?
back: A quota can only tie a tariff's welfare loss (B+D) if the rent is captured domestically (e.g., via license auction); it is never strictly better for the importing country.

front: Supplementary: Reasons governments impose trade restrictions?
back: Protect established or infant domestic industries, protect employment, protect strategic industries for national security, raise government revenue, or retaliate against another country's restrictions.
Only the portion of new member imports that displaces prior domestic production counts as trade creation — not the full increase in imports, part of which is new consumption.

front: Supplementary: Tell for trade diversion in a scenario?
back: A country switches import sources after a bloc forms, away from a non-member that was genuinely cheaper before any tariffs existed, toward a tariff-free member.

front: Supplementary: Why is regional integration more popular than multilateral (WTO) negotiation?
back: Eliminating barriers among a small group of countries is politically less contentious and faster to negotiate and coordinate than multilateral trade negotiation.

front: Supplementary: National-sovereignty concern in bloc formation?
back: Especially salient when very differently sized economies join the same bloc, over fear the larger economy's preferences will dominate shared decisions.
Persistent imbalances are harder to correct without independent monetary policy or currency devaluation, so a crisis in one member can spread to others facing similar problems.
